You might be keen about an idea, yet you feel no one is listening. (There are none so deaf as those who are wearing headphones.) Be patient with family members. It's easy to feel disappointed with someone today.</p><h2>Aquarius (Jan. 20-Feb. 18)</h2> <p></p> <div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="HtmlModule"><a class="AnchorLink" id="html-embed-module-4d0000" name="html-embed-module-4d0000"></a><div class="HoroscopeStarbox HoroscopeStarbox_five"> <div class="HoroscopeStarbox_container"> <svg class="HoroscopeStar"><use xlink:href="#icon-star"></use></svg> <svg class="HoroscopeStar"><use xlink:href="#icon-star"></use></svg> <svg class="HoroscopeStar"><use xlink:href="#icon-star"></use></svg> </div> <div class="HoroscopeStarbox_description"> <p>An <b>average</b> day</p> </div> </div> <style> .HoroscopeStarbox { background: #f8f8f8; display: flex; align-items: center; } .HoroscopeStarbox_container { display: grid; grid-gap: 5px; grid-template-columns: 1fr 1fr 1fr 1fr 1fr; padding: 20px; width: 40%; min-width: 160px; max-width: 200px; } .HoroscopeStarbox_description { padding: 20px; font-family: var(--font-1); font-size: var(--body-2); } .HoroscopeStarbox_container svg { object-fit: cover; aspect-ratio: 1 / 1; width: 100%; } </style> </div> </div><p> You want to save the world before bedtime. Perhaps today you're on your soapbox urging others to listen to your ideas because you feel it's important to be heard. You might be right, but if you're obsessed with something, people will turn away. (You know this.)</p><h2>Pisces (Feb. 19-March 20)</h2> <p></p> <div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="HtmlModule"><a class="AnchorLink" id="html-embed-module-290000" name="html-embed-module-290000"></a><div class="HoroscopeStarbox HoroscopeStarbox_five"> <div class="HoroscopeStarbox_container"> <svg class="HoroscopeStar"><use xlink:href="#icon-star"></use></svg> <svg class="HoroscopeStar"><use xlink:href="#icon-star"></use></svg> </div> <div class="HoroscopeStarbox_description"> <p>A <b>so-so</b> day</p> </div> </div> <style> .HoroscopeStarbox { background: #f8f8f8; display: flex; align-items: center; } .HoroscopeStarbox_container { display: grid; grid-gap: 5px; grid-template-columns: 1fr 1fr 1fr 1fr 1fr; padding: 20px; width: 40%; min-width: 160px; max-width: 200px; } .HoroscopeStarbox_description { padding: 20px; font-family: var(--font-1); font-size: var(--body-2); } .HoroscopeStarbox_container svg { object-fit: cover; aspect-ratio: 1 / 1; width: 100%; } </style> </div> </div><p> Financial discussions might be discouraging today. You might feel broke and no matter what happens, the light at the end of the tunnel looks like a train. Be reassured that this is a temporary dark cloud on your horizon. Courage!</p><h2>If today is your birthday</h2><p>Actress Meryl Streep (1949) shares your birthday today. You seek an enduring, romantic partnership — a perfect lifestyle. Finding true love is of paramount importance. This is a slower-paced year. Take time to rejuvenate your energy and outlook. Focus on business and personal relationships, and be with people who have your back. Be kind and helpful this year.</p>

entries.title: Brookfield Zoo is helping repopulate Bad Bunny concho
entries.summary: <p>Months after Super Bowl LX, Puerto Rico’s only native toad species is still having a moment thanks to Bad Bunny.</p><p>And with a little help from the Brookfield Zoo, that turn in the spotlight might just save the amphibian from extinction. </p><p>The singer’s mascot is named Concho, and it was created in the likeness of the endangered Puerto Rican crested toad. Bad Bunny, whose given name is Benito Antonio Martínez Ocasio, adopted the creature as a mascot and symbol of resilience, mirroring the toad’s struggles to stay alive with the displacement that islanders face today.</p><p>Known as the sapo concho in Spanish, the species is the Caribbean island’s only native toad. Years ago, the Puerto Rican Crested Toad Conservancy tapped the suburban Chicago zoo to breed thousands of tadpoles, but Brookfield hit a milestone this spring.</p><div class="Enhancement" entries.title: Bullets from Dan Ryan shootout shatters window of CTA train; glass shards injure passenger in Roseland
entries.summary: <p>A shootout among three vehicles traveling on the Dan Ryan Expressway left a CTA passenger to be hit by flying shards of glass when a bullet pierced the train's window Sunday afternoon in Roseland. </p><p>The passenger, a 46-year-old man, was riding the train in the first block of West 95th Street about 2:15 p.m. when a shootout among three vehicles nearby on the inbound Day Ryan Expressway erupted, police said. </p><p>When gunfire smashed the train's window, the man was hit in the face and body by glass. He was taken to Advocate Trinity Hospital, where he was in good condition. </p><p>The drivers of the shooting vehicles fled and have not been arrested. </p><p>Area 2 detectives are investigating. </p>

entries.title: City leaders: Tuning out, closing doors on youth won't solve problems
entries.summary: <p>For Chicago teens on the South and West sides, summer brings time with friends and a break from schoolwork. Sadly, it also brings the annual message from the Chicago City Council that we are not welcome in public spaces. We need a firm commitment to supporting young people, not repeated calls to lock us out and lock us up for gathering.</p><p>I am a youth organizer with GoodKids MadCity, where I work with young people from communities where gun violence is prevalent. We teach restorative justice and peacekeeping skills that allow young people to heal and resolve conflicts before they escalate into violence.</p><p>Programs like these are working. This <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2026/05/24/17-people-shot-overnight-chicago" >Memorial Day weekend</a> was the least violent since 2010. Despite this progress, many Chicago politicians continue to blame teens for any degree of disorder. They support “solutions” that criminalize young people and do nothing to address the underlying issues of minimal recreational opportunities, unemployment and underfunded community services.</p><p>Last summer, Ald. Brian Hopkins’ (2nd) “snap curfew” proposal, allowing for a curfew on young people at any time with only 30 minutes notice, thankfully <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/city-hall/2025/07/16/snap-curfew-veto-upheld-mayor-johnson-city-council-vote" >failed</a>. This year, Hopkins has a <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/city-hall/2026/01/21/brian-hopkins-curfew-ordinance-new-revision-mayor-brandon-johnson-teen-takeovers" >new effort</a> that would allow for “declarations of disruptive youth gatherings.” The intent is clear: more power and discretion for police to stop young people from gathering.</p><p>The city’s leaders should instead focus on promoting engagement for young people. In 2019, GoodKids MadCity hosted a free summer beach party at the 31st Street Beach that drew over 1,000 teenagers. No fights, shootings or other violence occurred, though recent stories would have our community believe teens are incapable of these kinds of peaceful gatherings.</p><p>Gun violence is an urgent issue demanding an immediate response. But the necessary response is youth-led peacekeeping, not curfews and parental “accountability” laws that fail to address the circumstances Chicago’s young people live in. City leaders need to abandon their penchant for punishment and turn toward caring for our community. They need to talk to the young people who will be affected by the city’s choices and listen closely to what they have to say.</p><p><i>Reynia Jackson, youth organizer, GoodKids MadCity</i></p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-c00000" name="module-c00000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h3>Give us your take</h3><br>Send letters to the editor to <a class="Link" href="mailto:letters@suntimes.com" target="_blank" >letters@suntimes.com</a>. To be considered for publication, letters must include your full name, your neighborhood or hometown and a phone number for verification purposes. Letters should be a maximum of approximately 375 words.</div> </div><p></p><h3><b>Protect 340B as a lifeline for patients, communities</b></h3><p>The Illinois General Assembly recently passed <a class="Link" href="https://www.ilga.gov/legislation/BillStatus?DocTypeID=HB&DocNum=2371&GAID=18&SessionID=114&LegID=160084" target="_blank" >House Bill 2371</a>, the Patient Access to Pharmacy Protection Act, to protect patient access to affordable medications and strengthen care for communities across Illinois.</p><p>For more than 30 years, the federal 340B drug pricing program has helped safety-net hospitals, health centers and clinics for patients most in need. Because Medicare and Medicaid often do not fully cover the cost of care, 340B allows organizations like Loyola Medicine to stretch limited resources further.</p><p>In exchange for providing discounts to safety-net providers for outpatient prescription drugs, pharmaceutical companies gain access to the Medicare and Medicaid markets, which cover about half of all Americans.</p><p>Loyola Medicine is one of those safety-net providers. We serve a disproportionate share of Medicaid and Medicare patients with complex needs, including burn, trauma and transplant care.</p><p>Nearly 3 in 4 of our patients rely on Medicare or Medicaid, and 2% have no insurance at all. The savings generated through 340B are not profits — they are reinvested into programs that improve access, enhance outcomes and strengthen the communities we serve.</p><p>For example, Loyola’s Meds to Beds program ensures patients leave the hospital with prescriptions in hand and clear instructions from a pharmacist. This program has reduced readmissions by 44%, helping patients stay healthier while lowering overall health care costs.</p><p>Today, that lifeline is at risk. Pharmaceutical companies have increasingly restricted access to 340B discounts, particularly through contract pharmacies that help patients obtain medications close to home. These actions threaten access for seniors, patients with low incomes and those in underserved communities.</p><p>House Bill 2371 offers an important solution by protecting these pharmacy relationships and ensuring Illinois residents can access medications where they live.</p><p>Hospitals qualify for 340B because they serve a higher proportion of low-income and medically complex patients — individuals more likely to be uninsured or managing chronic conditions. Without these resources, we would face difficult choices — scaling back services, limiting access or eliminating programs — forcing patients to travel farther or forgo care.</p><p>We urge Gov. JB Pritzker to act now and sign HB 2371 to protect patients, preserve access to care and ensure hospitals can continue serving those who need it most.</p><p>Protect 340B. Protect patients.</p><p><i>DeRondal Bevly, board chair, Loyola Medicine</i></p><h3>Visit to Chicago essential with Obama Presidential Center</h3><p>With the long anticipated <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/arts-and-culture/2026/06/16/obama-presidential-center" >opening</a> of the Obama Presidential Center, I can't personally think of a better time than to be in the <a class="Link" href="https://worldpopulationreview.com/us-cities" target="_blank" >third most populous city</a> in the United States this summer. Yes, Chicago is my kind of town.</p><p>The nostalgia from last week's opening is too overwhelming to ignore. The selected works of art, particularly the unveiling of <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/art/2026/06/16/portrait-akunyili-crosby-obamas-life-story-debuts-obama-presidential-center" >Njideka Akunyili Crosby’s</a> commissioned portrait, makes planning a trip to Chicago more exciting. From what I've seen from afar, visiting Chicago is surely on my bucket list. Welcome Obama Presidential Center!</p><p><i>Wayne E. Williams, Camden, New Jersey</i></p><h3>Boomerang Bears?</h3><p>I'm not from Chicago but have lived both in Illinois and Indiana (one-time employee of the Chicago Tribune, in full disclosure), so I thought I'd offer an outsider's, "non-sports guy" point on the prospective Bears relocation to northwest Indiana.</p><p>During my time growing up in and around Washington, D.C., the Redskins played at RFK Stadium, maybe a mile or two due east of the U.S. Capitol. The team, now known as the Commanders, play at Northwest Stadium in Landover, Maryland. However, the plan as I understand it, is that the team will return to a new stadium at the <a class="Link" href="https://www.commanders.com/news/mayor-bowser-and-washington-commanders-announce-historic-deal-to-bring-the-team-home" target="_blank" >RFK campus</a>, circa 2030.</p><p>So could this be a harbinger of what's to come? Homesick Bears at some point? Maybe holding at the 50-yard line, in a manner of speaking, is the best option.</p><p><i>Steve Wilson, Madison</i></p>

entries.title: As Trump hacks away at environmental protections, Illinois strengthens them
entries.summary: <p>Americans are less safe and healthy today because of the Trump administration.</p><p>This time will be defined in part by a legacy of curtailing bedrock environmental protections, including <a class="Link" href="https://apnews.com/article/trump-epa-endangerment-climate-change-public-health-25764e8298db96c3c189b6833252b7ca" target="_blank" >rescinding</a> the U.S. EPA’s greenhouse gas endangerment finding, <a class="Link" href="https://www.cnn.com/2026/02/22/business/car-emissions-regulations-trump" target="_blank" >weakening</a> vehicle emissions standards, <a class="Link" href="https://www.nytimes.com/2025/02/19/climate/army-corps-engineers-fossil-fuel-permits.html?unlocked_article_code=1.rFA.q7_l.Y56oVOoCv_Hv&smid=url-share" target="_blank" >accelerating</a> fossil fuel permitting and, most recently, <a class="Link" href="https://abcnews.com/US/epa-proposes-limits-clean-water-act/story?id=127645448" target="_blank" >curtailing</a> clean water protections, all in an increasingly <a class="Link" href="https://science.nasa.gov/climate-change/evidence/" target="_blank" >warming world</a>.</p><p>They’re trading off our long-term health to scratch the backs of big polluters for short-term profits, and the uncomfortable truth is Americans will die as a result.</p><p>It’s a different story here in Illinois, where we’ve chosen a path grounded in science, public health and the understanding that clean air and clean water keep life more affordable for average Illinoisans. In stark contrast to Trump, Gov. JB Pritzker and his administration — especially Illinois Environmental Protection Agency Director James Jennings — have built one of the strongest state-level environmental records in the country. Together, they’re effectively inoculating Illinoisans from some of the worst environmental impacts.</p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-370000" name="module-370000"></a> <div class="RichTextSidebarModule-title">Commentary bug</div> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h2>Commentary</h2></div> </div><p>This leadership has become increasingly important. For example, the Trump administration recently announced its intention to <a class="Link" href="https://www.epa.gov/newsreleases/epa-announces-it-will-keep-maximum-contaminant-levels-pfoa-pfos?utm_source=chatgpt.com" target="_blank" >roll back</a> protective national drinking water standards for toxic Per- and Polyfluoroalkyl substances, known as PFAS, in community water supplies. Now found in drinking water, wildlife and even human bloodstream, these “forever chemicals” are linked to cancer, immune system suppression and developmental harms.</p><p>Not only has the state moved aggressively to address PFAS since 2020, but this legislative session, the Pritzker administration and Illinois EPA advanced <a class="Link" href="https://ilga.gov/Legislation/BillStatus?DocNum=5070&GAID=18&DocTypeID=HB&LegId=166584&SessionID=114" target="_blank" >legislation</a>, sponsored by state Sen. Laura Ellman and state Rep. Ann Williams, to end the automatic adoption of weakened federal environmental standards in Illinois.</p><p>Now, Illinois will keep its superior PFAS standards in place.</p><p>The Trump administration has also <a class="Link" href="https://www.ucs.org/about/news/trump-administration-rolls-back-ethylene-oxide-rules" target="_blank" >rolled back</a> ethylene oxide regulations. Ethylene oxide is a cancer-causing air pollutant. In Illinois, the horrific Sterigenics <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/2023/1/9/23547780/sterigenics-to-pay-408-million-settle-hundreds-of-lawsuits-over-toxic-gas-emissions" >contamination crisis</a> in Willowbrook, near my hometown of Darien, led to stronger state protections championed by Illinois Senate Minority Leader John Curran, R-Downers Grove.</p><p>Because of those protections, facilities operating under the dangerous standards of the past will not reopen in Illinois, regardless of Trump rollbacks.</p><p>Coal ash is one of the most dangerous toxic legacies of the fossil fuel industry. Trump’s team has taken several steps away from faster, stronger cleanup and stricter monitoring of coal ash contamination, to giving utilities more time, narrower obligations and more cleanup exemptions. This spring, they <a class="Link" href="https://apnews.com/article/trump-coal-climate-fossil-fuels-industry-emissions-862c3f0722d6ebc847bd49b2196cf9a9" target="_blank" >proposed to roll back</a> essential federal coal ash protections, leaving hundreds of communities vulnerable to toxic pollution.</p><p>Luckily, the Illinois General Assembly has led on this issue, too. Illinois adopted one of the nation’s strongest <a class="Link" href="https://ipmnewsroom.org/coal-ash-is-polluting-illinois-rivers-environmentalists-want-the-state-to-move-faster-to-stop-it/" target="_blank" >coal ash laws</a>, requiring groundwater monitoring, closure standards, transparency and stronger protections for nearby communities. The governor’s environmental agency will need to strongly implement and enforce these in the face of federal challenges.</p><p>The Trump administration has largely dismantled or deprioritized the federal infrastructure built to address disproportionate pollution burdens in low-income communities and communities of color. The While the Pritzker administration has strengthened environmental justice protections by advancing policies that address cumulative pollution impacts in communities that have historically borne the greatest environmental burdens, the federal government retreats from this work.</p><p>Big polluters should pay the cost of pollution prevention; no one should be paying that cost with their health, their means or their lives.</p><p>Across the country, states are forced to decide whether they will wait for Washington or lead themselves. Illinois has consistently chosen leadership.</p><p>That leadership matters. Strong environmental laws are not abstract policy victories. They are the reason a child drinks safer water, a family breathes cleaner air and communities avoid devastating toxic contamination.</p><p>None of that would be possible without the incredible scientists and environmental experts who proudly call Illinois home. They’re the backbone of these policy victories and the architects of the decades of groundwork that got us here.</p><p>Together, those of us invested in the work of safeguarding Illinois, our people, wildlife and ecosystems will continue to celebrate the progress Pritzker and his state agencies are making, and in some cases, push those leaders to continue building on this increasingly impressive record of environmental protection.</p><p><i>Jen Walling is CEO of the Illinois Environmental Council.</i></p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-f30000" name="module-f30000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody">Send letters to <a class="Link" href="mailto:letters@suntimes.com" target="_blank" >letters@suntimes.com</a>. More about <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/submitting-opinion-and-letters" >how to submit here</a>.</div> </div><p></p>

entries.title: Dear Abby: Once married, wife realizes her husband is someone else
entries.summary: <p><b>DEAR ABBY:</b> I have experienced something that other women I know have said they have also experienced. I dated a man for a year. We became very close and fell in love. He was sweet, loving and kind in every way. Before I would commit to marriage, I made sure we had discussions about respect and what I expected from a life partner.</p><p>The change in my (now) husband was instantaneous with our marriage and severe. He became someone I didn't know and never would have married. He is argumentative, petty and a bully. I feel as if I've been lied to. What happened? — <i>CONFOUNDED IN OREGON</i></p><p><b>DEAR CONFOUNDED:</b> What happened is while your husband was courting you, he put only his best foot forward, concealing who he really is. If the person he now shows himself to be isn't someone you would have married, end the emotional abuse and the bullying by ensuring he can't hide assets to which you may be entitled and talking to a lawyer about freeing yourself from this marriage to a stranger.</p><p><b>DEAR ABBY:</b> I'm a divorced father of a 27-year-old daughter. I recently found out she is being married in four months. Of course, I couldn't be happier.</p><p>I told my daughter that although I am not rich by any means, I would be glad to chip in what I could for her wedding. When I asked if I could invite a few friends and their spouses, she said I could, but I would have to pay for their plates. I was shocked. What do I do or say? — <i>DISAPPOINTED DAD IN NEW JERSEY</i></p><p><b>DEAR DAD:</b> Your daughter, the happy bride, is the person who gets to set the rules for her wedding. Because you learned about her wedding only after the plans were set, I sense there may have been some estrangement. You were generous to offer to help defray the expenses of the celebration, but if you want to include your friends, you will have to pay for the additional cost of feeding them. Perhaps some of your contribution could be earmarked to cover this expense.</p><p><b>DEAR ABBY:</b> I have a co-worker who eats canned sardines on top of his salad every day. I know they are high in protein and could be considered healthy, but they stink. He already covers his salad with red onion and balsamic vinegar, and the smell almost takes me out. If that's not bad enough, he literally slurps the remaining oil after he has finished the salad.</p><p>How should I tell him it stinks, or at least ask him to stop drinking the oil like it's water? — <i>SMELLS FISHY IN IOWA</i></p><p><b>DEAR SMELLS:</b> You didn't mention where this feast for the senses is taking place. Is there no way to distance yourself from the stench or stagger your lunch breaks so as to avoid the situation?</p><p>If not, you may want to rally support from other co-workers who feel the same and approach your supervisor or human resources. Ask that a rule be enacted about strong-smelling foods in shared spaces. HR should be able to work out a compromise that allows everyone to enjoy their lunch in peace.</p><p><i>Dear Abby is written by Abigail Van Buren, also known as Jeanne Phillips, and was founded by her mother, Pauline Phillips. Contact Dear Abby at www.DearAbby.com or P.O. Box 446, Kings Mills, OH 45034-0446. (Shipping and handling are included in the price.)</p>

entries.title: Bears set start of training camp, joint practices with Bengals, Titans
entries.summary: <p>The <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears" target="_blank" >Bears</a> will report for training camp July 28 and begin practice the next day, the team announced Monday. They also have confirmed joint practices with the Bengals and Titans in August.</p><p>Teams' reporting dates are tied to their season opener and whether they're playing in the Hall of Fame Game in the preseason, and the Bears have a fairly conventional schedule this season. Their first preseason game is Aug. 15 at home against the Browns, and their Week 1 game is Sept. 13 at the Panthers.</p><p>Quarterbacks and rookies will arrive at least a few days ahead of the rest of the team.</p><p>The Bears will play a preseason game at the Bengals on Aug. 22 and at the Titans on Aug. 29 — all of their preseason games are on Saturdays — and will do one practice with each of those teams two days before the game. Teams often emphasize those joint practices over the actual preseason games, though coach Ben Johnson didn't sit starters in those scenarios last season after joint practices with the Dolphins and <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears/2024/08/08/bears-to-play-starters-including-qb-caleb-williams-making-his-debut-in-preseason-game-vs-bills" >Bills</a>.</p><p>All joint practices are open to the public. The Bears plan to release their full training camp schedule, including open practices at Halas Hall, this week.</p>

entries.title: White Sox activate catcher Kyle Teel from rehab assignment ahead of Guardians series
entries.summary: <p>The White Sox are getting back a big bat just in time for a big series.</p><p>The team activated catcher Kyle Teel from the injured list Monday ahead of its series against the American League Central-leading Guardians, who are one game ahead of the Sox. Edgar Quero was optioned to Triple-A Charlotte. </p><p>Teel is returning from two injury rehab assignments. First, he strained his right hamstring during the World Baseball Classic on March 10. While on a rehab assignment for that injury, he sprained a knee ligament May 16. The Sox moved him to the 60-day injured list, leaving the 40-man roster at 39. He now retakes that open spot.</p><p>On his second rehab, Teel played in four games for the Knights, going 8-for-16 with one home run, four RBI and five runs scored. He went 5-for-6 on Friday at Buffalo. Last season, his first with the Sox, Teel had a .786 OPS with eight homers and 35 RBI. He led the team in batting average (.288) and on-base percentage (.376) after the All-Star break.</p><p>Quero has had a rough second big-league season, slashing .187/.253/.233 with two home runs, 15 RBI and 12 runs scored in 55 games. Sox catchers, also including Drew Romo and former Sox Reese McGuire, have combined for major-league lows of a .167 batting average and a .241 on-base percentage. entries.title: 8 dead, dozens hurt including 14 shot during Juneteenth party over holiday weekend in Chicago
entries.summary: <p>A 14-year-old boy was among eight people killed over the long holiday weekend that saw nearly 40 others wounded, including 14 people shot during a Juneteenth celebration on the Far South Side. </p><p>Marcus Chatman, 14, <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2026/06/19/auburn-gresham-shooting" target="_blank" >was shot multiple times around 11:30 p.m.</a> Thursday in the 8000 block of South Carpenter Street in Auburn Gresham, Chicago police and the Cook County medical examiner's office said. </p><p>Marcus played for the Midwest Hawks youth football team in Country Club Hills.</p><p>“Though his life was taken far too soon, his memory will forever remain a part of the Midwest Hawks family," the team said in a statement.</p><p><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/news/2026/06/20/5-dead-19-hurt-in-weekend-shootings-including-12-wounded-in-mass-shooting" target="_blank" >A mass shooting in Roseland happened Friday</a> about 11:10 p.m. in the 200 block of West 95th Street as a large crowd gathered for the holiday. A red SUV drove by and two people inside opened fire, hitting the 14 victims, whose ages ranged from 17 to 47.</p><p>That shooting caught the attention of President Donald Trump, who posted on social media: "Lots of Killing going on in Chicago. 22 people shot, at least 4 Dead. Why isn't Governor Pritzker calling me for help."</p><p>Seven others killed from Thursday 5 p.m. until Monday at 5 a.m., according to officials. They include:<br></p><ul class="rte2-style-ul" id="rte-d3e27c22-6e5f-11f1-8283-d55b6e70bbb7"><li>Christopher A. Lakes, 34, shot in Austin; </li><li>Aniyhas S. Jackson, 18, shot in Austin; </li><li>a 21-year-old man shot in the 5500 block of South Princeton Avenue in Englewood; </li><li>a 37-year-old man shot in the 500 block of East 38th Street in Bronzeville; </li><li>a 33-year-old man shot in the 3000 block of West 30th Street in Little Village; </li><li><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2026/06/19/man-fatally-shot-west-pullman-another-injured" target="_blank" >a 29-year-old man shot</a> in the 11900 block of South Michigan Avenue in West Pullman; </li><li>a 32-year-old man shot in the 600 block of East 92nd Street in Chatham.</li></ul><p>Other <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/news/2026/06/21/overnight-violence-chicago-teens-shot" target="_blank" >shootings wounded nearly 20 others </a> in neighborhoods on the South and West Sides, according to Chicago police. </p>

entries.title: Motoryclist killed in collision with SUV in Mount Prospect
entries.summary: <p>A 20-year-old Des Plaines man died after his motorcycle collided with a Subaru SUV on Saturday night in Mount Prospect. </p><p>Police said an officer discovered the wreck on Rand Road near Henry Street at about 10:01 p.m. The officer found the motorcycle driver, later identified as Scotty J. Stuck, southeast of the intersection with serious injuries, according to Mount Prospect police. </p><p>Stuck was taken to Advocate Lutheran General Hospital in Park Ridge by the Mount Prospect Fire Department, where he was pronounced dead at 11:53 p.m., according to the Cook County medical examiner's office. </p><p>A 33-year-old Mount Prospect man driving the SUV and was not injured as a result of the crash, police said.</p><p>Authorities are investigating the cause of the crash and police ask hat anyone with information regarding the crash contact the department’s Major Crash Investigation Team at <a class="Link" href="tel:8478185301" target="_blank" >847-818-5301</a>.</p>

entries.title: West Suburban Medical Center could lose power next month because of unpaid electric bill
entries.summary: <p>West Suburban Medical Center might have its power shut off next month because the owner is behind on electric bill payments. </p><p>ComEd posted a notice on the Oak Park hospital's doors earlier this month, warning that the power will be turned off on July 8 if the owner doesn't catch up on payments. The issue came up Monday during a hearing in Cook County court in the ongoing legal battle between its two owners. </p><p>The beleaguered hospital was recently shut down by the village of Oak Park because all 28 of its elevators have stopped working. The village's fire department was called to West Suburban on June 11 because patients coming in for appointments couldn't reach the clinics on the top floors of the hospital or return to the ground floor, according to a village spokesperson. </p><p>Oak Park is requiring the hospital to repair at least two elevators before it can reopen. That has yet to happen, the spokesperson said. </p><p>Representatives for the hospital's owners, Manoj Prasad and Rathnakar Reddy Patlola, did not immediately respond to requests for comment. A ComEd spokesperson did not immediately respond to a request for comment. </p><p>Prasad is the CEO and majority owner of Resilience Healthcare, which owns West Suburban, West Suburban’s River Forest medical campus and Weiss Memorial Hospital in Chicago's Uptown neighborhood. Patlola is the minority owner of Resilience and the landlord for all three hospital properties. </p><p>Citing issues with the hospital's billing system, Prasad abruptly closed West Suburban in March. He reopened <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/health/2026/04/15/west-suburban-medical-center-reopening-some-clinics-amid-eviction-fight" target="_blank" >some outpatient clinics back in April</a>. PCC Community Wellness Center operates its own clinics at West Suburban and had remained opened up until the elevators failed. </p><p>The decision to close the hospital <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/health/2026/05/26/west-suburban-medical-center-oak-park-prasad-patlola-resilience-healthcare" target="_blank" >triggered a legal battle</a> between Prasad and Patlola. </p><p>Patlola tried to oust Prasad and evict Resilience from both hospitals and the associated medical office buildings. Prasad then filed suit against Patlola to stop the eviction. In response, Patlola countersued, asking a judge to appoint a receiver to take control of West Suburban’s operations, allowing it to reopen. </p><p>Three weeks ago,<a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/health/2026/06/01/west-suburban-medical-center-owner-can-keep-control-of-hospital-judge-rules" target="_blank" > Judge Patrick Stanton ruled against</a> Patlola’s emergency request for a receiver, saying his lawyers did not meet the burden of proof.</p><p>During Monday's hearing, Stanton once again stressed the need for a plan to reopen the hospital. Lawyers for Prasad and Patlola are scheduled to return to court Thursday morning to continue hashing out a settlement plan to do just that. </p>

entries.title: Terminal de Greyhound en el centro de Chicago será de propiedad pública tras la aprobación de $19 millones
entries.summary: <p>La Ciudad de Chicago podría estar funcionando su primera terminal de autobuses interurbanos bajo propiedad pública para fines del verano, tras una votación del Concejo Municipal para comprar la deteriorada estación Greyhound ubicada en el South Loop.</p><p>La ordenanza aprobada el miércoles permite a la Municipalidad adquirir la terminal en 630 W. Harrison St. por $19 millones. El acuerdo también destina millones a la renovación de la terminal descuidada, y evita que las casi medio millón de personas que utilizan la estación cada año sean potencialmente trasladadas a un servicio de autobús en la acera.</p><p>El concejal Bill Conway (34.º) fue en su momento un escéptico de mantener la estación en su ubicación actual debido a preocupaciones sobre el crimen, el tráfico y el uso de fondos de financiamiento por el incremento de impuestos.</p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-2d0000" name="module-2d0000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h3>La Voz Chicago WhatsApp</h3>Encuentra más noticias en nuestro canal de WhatsApp. <a class="Link" href="https://www.whatsapp.com/channel/0029Vb0XT1XCHDylm3rCs40P" target="_blank" ><b>Síguenos.</b></a></div> </div><p>Dijo a los miembros del Concejo el miércoles que había cambiado de opinión tras considerar la importancia de mantener una terminal de autobuses interurbanos para sus usuarios de bajos ingresos, algunos de los cuales la utilizan para acceder a atención reproductiva en Illinois.</p><p>"Hacer nada dejará a los pasajeros sin estación de autobuses, o en el mejor de los casos, esperando en la parada afuera con un gran sitio en deterioro en la calle Harrison", comentó Conway.</p><p>La votación puso fin a un esfuerzo de varios años para evitar que Greyhound fuera desalojado de su propia terminal. Greyhound perdió la propiedad de la terminal hace cuatro años cuando la empresa vendió docenas de sus propiedades durante su adquisición por FlixBus.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-020000" name="image-020000"></a> <picture data-crop="medium"> <source type="image/webp" width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/f5da705/2147483647/strip/true/crop/6122x3436+0+324/resize/490x275!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F20%2F45%2Fefee1ad45d2e8dcc8e8f2528ceef%2Fmerlin-112954096.jpg 1x,https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/bff6148/2147483647/strip/true/crop/6122x3436+0+324/resize/980x550!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F20%2F45%2Fefee1ad45d2e8dcc8e8f2528ceef%2Fmerlin-112954096.jpg 2x" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <source width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/0d36a91/2147483647/strip/true/crop/6122x3436+0+324/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F20%2F45%2Fefee1ad45d2e8dcc8e8f2528ceef%2Fmerlin-112954096.jpg" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <img class="Image" alt="La terminal de autobuses de Greyhound está en 630 W. Harrison St., en el West Loop.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Anthony Vazquez/Sun-Times</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>El alcalde Brandon Johnson presentó la ordenanza para finalizar la compra, argumentando en el lenguaje de la ordenanza que comprar la estación era más barato que permitir el desalojo de Greyhound y construir una terminal de autobuses de propiedad municipal en otro lugar.</p><p>La compra por parte de la Municipalidad del actual propietario Alden Global Capital podría finalizarse en agosto, dijeron funcionarios de la ciudad la semana pasada, <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/transportation/2026/06/10/greyhound-bus-station-intercity-terminal-city-purchase-council-committee-approval" target="_blank" >cuando un comité avanzó la ordenanza</a>.</p><p>Johnson, hablando con reporteros tras la votación, dijo que "no iba a quedarse de brazos cruzados" mientras "una firma de capital privado... retiraba su apoyo a algo que los más vulnerables entre nosotros necesitan".</p><p>El propietario actual inicialmente planeó derribar la terminal y construir un rascacielos, pero finalmente llegó a un acuerdo con la Municipalidad para venderle el terreno.</p><p>El concejal Marty Quinn (13.º) se opuso al acuerdo, argumentando a sus colegas que el precio real para la Municipalidad superaba los $50 millones al considerar el trabajo adicional necesario por parte del Departamento de Transporte de la ciudad. Dijo que dudaba de que la Municipalidad pudiera operar una estación de autobuses pública y afirmó que el dinero podría ser utilizado en otros lugares.</p><p>La Municipalidad argumentó que la terminal se operará como cualquier aeropuerto gestionado por la Municipalidad; los operadores de autobuses pagarán un alquiler por usar la estación, y se espera que ello cubra los gastos operativos.</p><p>Como parte del acuerdo, FlixBus Norteamérica, que posee Greyhound, continuaría operando la estación durante un periodo de transición de 12 meses.</p><p>El precio de compra de $19 millones está por debajo del precio de mercado de $26 millones. Esto deja $31 millones en fondos de la Municipalidad para reparaciones y mejoras a la terminal descuidada.</p><p>La semana pasada, cuando el comité de bienes raíces del Concejo Municipal avanzó con la compra, los funcionarios dijeron que la Municipalidad primero reemplazaría el sistema de calefacción y refrigeración de la terminal, así como implementaría medidas como nuevas cámaras y mayor seguridad.</p><p><i>Traducido con una herramienta de inteligencia artificial (AI) y editado por </i><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/la-voz" target="_blank" ><i>La Voz Chicago</i></a></p>

entries.title: South Side, or Hammond, should beat Arlington Heights for Bears, state Rep. Curtis Tarver says
entries.summary: <p>Chicago should fight to keep the Bears. The Bears have said Arlington Heights and Hammond, Indiana, are the only viable sites and have taken another step toward Hammond. <a class="Link" href="https://abc7chicago.com/post/chicago-bears-held-meetings-terms-new-lakefront-stadium-mayor-brandon-johnsons-office-says/" target="_blank" >City Hall still insists</a> Chicago remains in the running through its lakefront proposal. </p><p>That conflict is why both sides should look farther south. City Hall has offered no serious plan to connect the Bears to its originally desired site, so why not try South Works or the South Lakefront?</p><p>The existing Museum Campus is one of Chicago's strongest assets. It already has world-class institutions, tourists, infrastructure and public attention. Directing another massive public effort there would reinforce an area already central to Chicago's civic life, while the Southeast Side is told, again, to wait.</p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-f60000" name="module-f60000"></a> <div class="RichTextSidebarModule-title">Commentary bug</div> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h2>Commentary</h2></div> </div><p>I am asking the Bears to give South Works and the South Lakefront a full, serious feasibility review. Envision a Museum Campus South plus Quantum. This is a vision we can build upon rather than displace. We can connect world-class museums, sports, science, health care, education, lakefront access, jobs, small businesses and neighborhood revival. That would be a citywide development strategy, not old Chicago with new renderings.</p><p>Gov. JB Pritzker and the General Assembly committed <a class="Link" href="https://capitolnewsillinois.com/news/ibm-will-bring-innovation-hub-750-new-jobs-to-chicagos-quantum-park/" target="_blank" >$500 million</a> to quantum development, with $300 million directed toward the South Works campus. PsiQuantum is anchoring the site and has begun <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/real-estate/2025/10/01/related-midwest-crg-breaks-ground-illinois-quantum-computing-park-us-steel-south-works" >construction</a>. Advocate Health Care is making a separate $1 billion South Side investment, including a $300 million hospital at the former U.S. Steel site.</p><p>City Council members Greg Mitchell (7th) and Peter Chico (10th) deserve special credit. They have championed these projects and pressed to ensure that health care, jobs, workforce opportunities and lasting investment reach residents who have waited decades. They are doing the local work of turning long-neglected land into opportunity.</p><h3>Where’s City Hall’s commitment to SE Side?</h3><h3></h3><p>The state has stepped up. The private sector has stepped up. City Hall has not matched that commitment.</p><p>Mayor Brandon Johnson's commitment to the site has been $5 million from the housing and economic development bond program. Five million dollars for a project intended to help define the next generation of Illinois economic development and generate upwards of $20 billion in economic opportunity.</p><p>The financing choices make the contrast sharper. City Hall swept a record $1.01 billion from tax increment financing<a class="Link" href="https://www.civicfed.org/chicagos-fy2026-adopted-budget" target="_blank" > districts </a>for 2026, yet the city itself received only about 23%. TIF exists to support redevelopment, infrastructure and capital projects. City Hall also authorized <a class="Link" href="https://news.wttw.com/2024/04/19/city-council-votes-32-17-borrow-125b-fund-economic-development-affordable-housing" target="_blank" >$1.25 billion</a> in borrowing for housing and economic development. With interest, the plan is expected to cost about $2.4 billion over 37 years.</p><p>Southeast Side residents will shoulder that long-term city debt like every other Chicagoan, while City Hall's reported direct commitment to the quantum park remains $5 million.</p><p>When City Hall wants to support other areas, the tools appear. A city panel backed $201.6 million in <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/real-estate/2026/06/09/city-panel-community-development-commission-201-6-million-tif-subsidy-foundry-park" >TIF assistance</a> for Foundry Park on the North Side. The City Council approved a $54.7 million <a class="Link" href="https://www.chicago.gov/city/en/depts/dcd/provdrs/ec_dev/news/2026/may/property-tax-incentive-will-support-phase-one-of-1901-project" target="_blank" >property tax incentive </a>for the first phase of the 1901 Project around the United Center. I am not arguing those projects should fail. I am arguing that the comparison reveals a priority problem.</p><p>A development anchored by the Bears in the South Works corridor could create a year-round destination, strengthen transit and infrastructure, support hotels, restaurants and small businesses, expand the local tax base and create accessible jobs for South Chicago and nearby communities. Done correctly, it could connect the Obama Presidential Center, the Griffin Museum of Science and Industry, Rainbow Beach, South Works, the quantum campus and the new Advocate hospital.</p><h3>Chicago first, then Hammond</h3><p>The Bears do not get a blank check. Any proposal must require significant private money, taxpayer protection, union jobs, strong minority and local hiring, workforce training, environmental safeguards, public lakefront access, neighborhood infrastructure and measurable economic returns for nearby residents.</p><p>The Southeast Side carried the steel industry, endured the pollution, lost the jobs and watched redevelopment promises come and go. It should not be asked to help finance development across Chicago while receiving a fraction of the attention and investment.</p><p>I am Chicago first. I want the Bears at South Works on the South Lakefront. I cannot support an Arlington Heights outcome that offers little meaningful benefit to the people I represent. If the Bears choose Hammond, my district would see some spillover because Hammond is close and connected to the Southeast Side. But why settle for spillover when the jobs, visitor spending, tax growth and surrounding development could be captured on the Chicago and Illinois side of the line?</p><p>The state of Illinois has acted. Gov. Pritzker has acted. Advocate and PsiQuantum have acted. Alds. Mitchell and Chico have acted. Residents are ready. Now City Hall and the Bears must finally look south.</p><p><i>State Rep. Curtis Tarver, D-Chicago, serves Illinois' 25th House District. He was first elected in 2018.</i> </p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-d50000" name="module-d50000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody">Send letters to <a class="Link" href="mailto:letters@suntimes.com" target="_blank" >letters@suntimes.com</a>. entries.title: Bulls find themselves in a rare power position in the 2026 NBA Draft
entries.summary: <p>Tiago Splitter has a dislike for labels.</p><p>The newly named Bulls head coach has his reasons.</p><p>“Foreign, big guy, 6'11, you don’t see many of those,” Splitter said of his own climb from former championship player to assistant coach, to now the leading man in that coaching chair. “So I was behind the bench in Houston with the Rockets, and I wanted to prove people wrong because sometimes we put labels like that. So that's the reason I went to Paris (to coach). I wanted to lead a team. I wanted to be a head coach, I wanted to get a group of guys where they didn’t expect them to be and get them better, and I did that in Paris.</p><p>“I came back to the NBA, stuff happened, got a chance to lead a team again (in Portland) and I did the same thing. I don’t like to put labels on people. I hate it when they put it on me.”</p><p>No wonder the days leading up to Tuesday’s first round of the NBA Draft must be somewhat irritating for Splitter because that’s all the league becomes this time of the year – a series of labels.</p><p>“Can’t miss,” “athletically challenged,” “unpolished …”</p><p>Projected No. 1 overall pick AJ Dybantsa has an inconsistent outside shot, projected No. 2 pick Darryn Peterson has an inconsistent motor. Cameron Boozer supposedly lacks a bit of athleticism, while projected No. 4 pick – where the Bulls currently reside – Caleb Wilson seems to have an allergy to making shots outside the paint.</p><p>Yet, as much as all of these prospects have been put under a microscope, the agreed assessment of the 2026 batch of players is this could prove to be one of the more talented, deepest draft classes since the vaunted 1996 class in which icons like Allen Iverson, Kobe Bryant, Ray Allen and Steve Nash came out of.</p><p>And the Bulls find themselves sitting in a rare position of drafting power.</p><p>Only Memphis has a slight edge up on the Bulls when it comes to draft pick value with the Grizzlies holding No. 3 overall, No. 16 and then No. 32 (the second pick in the second round).</p><p>Bulls executive vice president of basketball operations Bryson Graham has No. 4 overall, No. 15, and second rounders No. 38, and No. 56.</p><p>In other words, talent is coming to a Bulls team that is currently talent starved.</p><p>Who that is – specifically at No. 4 – remains the question, but fortunately for the Bulls there are four great answers.</p><p>While it is a deep draft, the top tier is a four-man race led by Dybantsa, Peterson, Boozer and Wilson. The latest intel has the Wizards going back and forth on either Dybantsa or Peterson at No. 1, but that could also be the shell game they are choosing to play.</p><p>Washington isn’t alone, either.</p><p>If it is Dybantsa at No. 1, Utah is also going with a smoke screen, making it very known that Boozer’s father – and one-time Bull – Carlos Boozer works as a scout/consultant for the organization.</p><p>Could Peterson and his baggage actually fall down to No. 4? It’s possible, and that’s why the Bulls are in such a position of power. They will get one of these big four no matter how the chess pieces are moved.</p><p>That’s why the Splitter hire was so important. Yes, he’s a big man that helped the development of Alperen Sengun while he was in Houston, but he also turned Trail Blazers point-forward Deni Avdija into an All-Star and somewhat resurrected the career of young guard Scoot Henderson.</p><p>Good news for Wilson, who only worked out for the Bulls, or for Peterson if he does slide a few spots.</p><p>As for No. 15 there are all kinds of names floating around with the Bulls, whether it’s Michigan big Aday Mara sliding to them, a two-way threat in Cameron Carr or a roughneck in Morez Johnson Jr., the franchise is set to add talent.</p><p>Unfortunately for Splitter, labels included.</p>

entries.title: Visitantes exploran el museo del Obama Presidential Center en el día de gran apertura
entries.summary: <p>Algunos se sintieron maravillados por la experiencia de sentarse detrás del escritorio en la réplica de la Oficina Oval del ex presidente.</p><p>Una visitante pensó en todas las personas que ayudaron a construir el lugar porque está casada con uno de ellos.</p><p>Y otros simplemente se sintieron abrumados al recordar lo que significó para ellos, y para el país, la elección del primer presidente negro.</p><p>Estas son sólo algunas de las reflexiones de los visitantes que tuvieron la suerte de conseguir las tan codiciadas entradas para el museo del Obama Presidential Center en su gran apertura.</p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-d90000" name="module-d90000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h3>La Voz Chicago WhatsApp</h3>Encuentra más noticias en nuestro canal de WhatsApp. <a class="Link" href="https://www.whatsapp.com/channel/0029Vb0XT1XCHDylm3rCs40P" target="_blank" ><b>Síguenos.</b></a></div> </div><p>Ellos formaron parte de miles de visitantes de todo el país que abarrotaron casi cada rincón del campus en Jackson Park el viernes para celebrar un lugar y a un presidente en Juneteenth.</p><h3>Delores Mcclendon, 45 años, Englewood</h3><p>Delores Mcclendon pasó horas recorriendo el museo, pero una instalación en particular le dio la oportunidad de revivir uno de los momentos más significativos no solo de su propia vida, sino de la vida de muchos otros también.</p><p>Mcclendon dijo que la exposición que más destacó fue un video que reproducía el día en que el expresidente Barack Obama ganó las elecciones presidenciales de 2008.</p><p>“Recuerdo esa noche, sentada allí viéndolo con mi familia”, dijo Mcclendon. “Todos estábamos llorando mientras él se acercaba cada vez más a la victoria. Estábamos celebrando”.</p><p>Pero antes de convertirse en presidente, Obama fue su vecino, comentó.</p><p>“Él es de Chicago y eso es lo más emocionante para mí”, contó Mcclendon. “Saber que alguien que creció en la misma comunidad y llegó tan lejos tuvo un gran impacto en nuestra nación es increíble”.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-cf7411" name="image-cf7411"></a> <picture data-crop="medium"> <source type="image/webp" width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/80c8f47/2147483647/strip/true/crop/6736x3780+0+355/resize/490x275!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Fe1%2Fbf%2Fbbfbe53546c8a42bbddac68aff3f%2Fopcvignettes-260620-12.jpg 1x,https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/4a565be/2147483647/strip/true/crop/6736x3780+0+355/resize/980x550!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Fe1%2Fbf%2Fbbfbe53546c8a42bbddac68aff3f%2Fopcvignettes-260620-12.jpg 2x" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <source width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/74350e4/2147483647/strip/true/crop/6736x3780+0+355/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Fe1%2Fbf%2Fbbfbe53546c8a42bbddac68aff3f%2Fopcvignettes-260620-12.jpg" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <img class="Image" alt="Delores Mcclendon, de Englewood, visitó el Museo del Obama Presidential Center en Juneteenth, su apertura pública. Ahora, viviendo en la capital del país, dijo que se sintió obligado a regresar a casa para presenciar la apertura “histórica” del Obama Presidential Center.</p><p>Tarver comentó que fue difícil elegir una exposición o instalación favorita porque, para él, el museo representa “lo mejor y lo más brillante que Estados Unidos tiene para ofrecer”.</p><p>El nativo de Chicago dijo que Obama fue “una fuerza de luz” que sigue brindando esperanza a las personas.</p><p>“El museo les dará a los jóvenes algo por lo que esperar”, dijo Tarver. “Les dará a los mayores algo por lo que seguir soñando. entries.title: Aseguran que ICE violó la ley estatal al detener a un hombre sin presentar una orden en la corte de Bridgeview
entries.summary: <p>Una coalición de 15 legisladores estatales está exigiendo respuestas de la Oficina del Sheriff del Condado de Cook después de que varias personas fueron detenidas por agentes del Servicio de Control de Inmigración y Aduanas (ICE) el miércoles en la corte del Condado de Cook en Bridgeview sin presentar una orden judicial.</p><p>El año pasado, el entonces Juez Principal del Circuito del Condado de Cook, Timothy Evans, firmó una orden <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/immigration/2025/10/14/top-cook-county-judge-bars-civil-arrests-at-courthouses-citing-chilling-effect" target="_blank" >prohibiendo las detenciones por cargos civiles</a> en y alrededor de las cortes del condado, aunque las órdenes judiciales aún pueden ejecutarse. Está respaldada por una ley estatal firmada en diciembre que prohíbe a los agentes federales realizar detenciones civiles en las cortes estatales, y la presidenta de la Junta del Condado de Cook, Toni Preckwinkle, también firmó una orden ejecutiva <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/la-voz/2025/10/17/preckwinkle-emite-orden-ejecutiva-para-crear-zonas-libres-de-ice-en-el-condado-de-cook" target="_blank" >prohibiendo a los federales realizar operativos en propiedades del condado</a> como lo hicieron <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/la-voz/2025/10/07/alcalde-johnson-firma-una-orden-ejecutiva-declarando-propiedades-de-la-ciudad-como-zonas-libres-de-ice" target="_blank" >Chicago</a> y otros.</p><p>Los 15 legisladores quieren que la oficina del alguacil proporcione sus protocolos para hacer cumplir todas esas medidas.</p><p>El miércoles, la Oficina del Sheriff del Condado de Cook dijo que un hombre corrió hacia la corte y a través de la seguridad, y fue detenido por los alguaciles antes de que los agentes de ICE ingresaran a la corte y lo esposaran. Dos personas intentaron filmar lo que ocurría cerca del control de seguridad, pero fueron detenidas por los alguaciles, según la oficina del sheriff.</p><p>Los agentes de ICE llevaron al hombre a un automóvil afuera y "le dijeron a un teniente que respondía en la Corte que tenían una orden de arresto válida", pero no presentaron ninguna, señaló la oficina del sheriff.</p><p>Un portavoz de ICE, que no proporcionó su nombre, dijo que tanto el hombre como la mujer eran venezolanos y tenían antecedentes penales por robo en tiendas. Según los registros judiciales, la mujer fue detenida cuando se dirigía a su primera audiencia en ese caso, y al hombre solo se le ha acusado de conducir sin licencia.</p><p>Cuando se le preguntó si los agentes violaron la ley estatal, el portavoz citó una declaración del Secretario de Seguridad Nacional, Markwayne Mullin, que amenazó con cortar los vuelos a ciudades santuario, y no abordó la pregunta de si los agentes tenían una orden.</p><p>Más temprano en el día, los agentes habían detenido a una mujer y a un niño pequeño cuando estaban a punto de ingresar a la corte, según la oficina del Defensor Público del Condado de Cook, que dijo que las detenciones eran "claras violaciones de la ley estatal". También dijeron que no habían podido encontrar cargos criminales federales para el hombre venezolano que fue arrestado más tarde, y que el hombre había estado en la corte para una audiencia en un caso en el que los fiscales planeaban ofrecer una suspensión de procesamiento.</p><p>Con base en un video publicado que muestra la detención, dijeron "no parece que la oficina del sheriff pidiera ver la orden".</p><p>"La conducta exhibida por los agentes federales fue ilegal y profundamente preocupante", dijo la oficina en un comunicado. "Como muestra claramente el video, se permitió a ICE arrestar a alguien en el vestíbulo de la corte a pesar de no presentar evidencia de cumplimiento de la ley estatal y una orden judicial... Detenciones como esta, que rutinariamente han involucrado a personas acusadas de delitos menores que en muchos casos son luego desestimados, dificultan el acceso a la justicia y dañan la confianza pública en nuestro sistema legal".</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center><div class="Enhancement-item"> <div class="ExternalContent-wrapper" > <div class="FacebookUrl"> <script>(function(d, s, id) { var js, fjs = d.getElementsByTagName(s)[0]; if (d.getElementById(id)) return; js = d.createElement(s); js.id = id; js.src = "//connect.facebook.net/en_US/sdk.js#xfbml=1&version=v20.0"; fjs.parentNode.insertBefore(js, fjs); }(document, 'script', 'facebook-jssdk'));</script><div class="fb-post" data-href="https://www.facebook.com/reel/1024996997135242"></div> </div> </div> </div></div><p>Rashid dijo que su oficina "gastaría todos los recursos" para investigar la detención. La interacción de un alguacil con un agente, así como la interacción de otro alguacil fuera de la corte con una de las personas que había estado filmando adentro, están siendo revisadas por la Oficina de Revisión Profesional del Sheriff.</p><p>Un <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/la-voz/2026/04/03/advierten-sobre-arrestos-de-ice-en-corte-de-violencia-domestica-afirman-que-agentes-estan-violando-la-ley" target="_blank" >número creciente de detenciones de ICE</a> en la Corte de Violencia Doméstica en el centro de Chicago a principios de este año fueron criticadas de manera similar por funcionarios públicos y activistas comunitarios.</p><p>Hacer responsables a los agentes de ICE por presuntas violaciones de leyes estatales y locales ha <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/la-voz/2026/05/26/jueza-del-condado-de-cook-rechaza-nombrar-fiscal-especial-para-investigar-agentes-de-operativo-midway-blitz" target="_blank" >resultado difícil en Illinois</a>, con funcionarios <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/immigration/2026/03/24/chicago-cook-county-trump-ice-border-patrol-midway-blitz-special-prosecutor-oneill-burke-loevy" target="_blank" >señalándose unos a otros</a>. Mientras tanto, los fiscales en estados como Minnesota han presentado cargos contra agentes federales por acciones similares a las de los agentes federales en Illinois, como <a class="Link" href="https://apnews.com/article/minneapolis-immigration-crackdown-charges-sosacelis-bd78efd7f341a9bd9c1acc2c0037a958" target="_blank" >dispararle a personas</a> o <a class="Link" href="https://apnews.com/article/immigration-minnesota-federal-officer-assault-charge-3083400c9b7d45fea4170a6abee7d290" target="_blank" >apuntarles con armas</a>.</p><p>Hatem Abudayyeh, director ejecutivo de la Red de Acción Árabe Estadounidense, dijo que aún cree que la presión para que se designe un fiscal especial que persiga a los agentes federales es la mejor opción para la rendición de cuentas. La Fiscal del Estado del Condado de Cook, Eileen O'Neill Burke, ha sido criticada por su falta de acción, pero un esfuerzo para que se designe un fiscal especial fue <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/la-voz/2026/05/26/jueza-del-condado-de-cook-rechaza-nombrar-fiscal-especial-para-investigar-agentes-de-operativo-midway-blitz" target="_blank" >rechazado por una jueza</a> en abril.</p><p>El grupo de Abudayyeh es parte de una red de respuesta rápida en los suburbios del suroeste que se presentó en la escena el miércoles en la corte de Bridgeview.</p><p>“No tengo ninguna confianza de que alguien más se involucre aquí. Los federales no se van a investigar a sí mismos”, dijo. “Solo puede detenerse por la gente de la comunidad resistiendo de la manera en que lo estamos haciendo, así que tenemos que seguir haciéndolo”.</p><p>La detención ocurre horas después de que el concejal Andre Vasquez (40.º) exigiera responsabilidad a la Policía de Chicago en un artículo de opinión del Chicago Tribune sobre los informes del Sun-Times acerca del <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/immigration/2026/06/05/ice-chicago-police-cpd-hit-and-run-crash-albany-park" target="_blank" >Departamento de Policía de Chicago (CDP) cerrando una investigación</a>sobre los agentes de ICE solo días después de que <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/la-voz/2026/06/03/agentes-de-ice-paralizan-a-un-hombre-con-taser-y-embisten-su-auto-en-un-arresto-caotico-en-albany-park" target="_blank" >chocaran el vehículo de una mujer</a> antes de utilizar un taser y detener a un hombre en Albany Park a principios de este mes.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center><div class="Enhancement-item"> <div class="ExternalContent-wrapper" data-embed> <iframe width="113" height="200" src="https://www.youtube.com/embed/ysQNeEB3ecE?feature=oembed" frameborder="0" allow="accelerometer; autoplay; clipboard-write; encrypted-media; gyroscope; picture-in-picture; web-share" referrerpolicy="strict-origin-when-cross-origin" allowfullscreen title="ICE agents shock man with Taser, barrel into car during chaotic arrest in Albany Park"></iframe> </div> </div></div><p>CPD no presentó un informe de incidente por el choque, un requisito cuando está involucrada una agencia de aplicación de la ley externa, de acuerdo con la orden ejecutiva del alcalde “ICE en Aviso”, lo que genera "preocupaciones de que [CPD] no ha activado completamente" esa orden, dijo Vasquez.</p><p>La oficina de la fiscal estatal del Condado de Cook ha argumentado que los fiscales no pueden actuar a menos que una agencia de policía realice una investigación y remita un caso para su revisión, lo que “hace que la manera en que CPD maneja este asunto sea aún más preocupante", dijo.</p><p>“Si un posible incidente de responsabilidad de la aplicación de la ley que involucra a agentes federales se reduce rápidamente a un informe de tráfico, etiquetado como ‘no criminal’ y suspendido en cuestión de días, entonces los fiscales nunca podrán recibir el tipo de expediente necesario para determinar si las acusaciones son justificadas”, escribió Vasquez.</p><p><i>Traducido con una herramienta de inteligencia artificial (AI) y editado por </i><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/la-voz" target="_blank" ><i>La Voz Chicago</i></a></p>

entries.title: Police looking for attacker in two South Shore sexual assaults
entries.summary: <p>Chicago police are looking for a man who allegedly sexually assaulted two women in South Shore earlier this month.</p><p>On June 13, a woman was alone in the 3100 block of East 79th Street around 6 a.m. when a man threw her to the ground and sexually assaulted her, police said in a community alert. Two days later around 8 p.m., another woman was in the 7700 block of S. South Shore Drive, around a half-mile away from the first reported assault, when the man assaulted her, police said. She fled after struggling with the man.</p><p>The attacker is described as a Black man around 30-40 years old and 5 foot 8 inches to 6 feet tall. He has medium complexion and short hair, police said.</p><p>Anyone with information on the reported assaults should contact Area Two Detectives at 312-747-8271 or submit an anonymous tip at CPDTIP.com and use reference #P26-02-010.</p>

entries.summary: <p>U.S. Attorney Andrew Boutros announced plans Monday<b> </b>to review nearly 20 years of grand jury proceedings involving a veteran prosecutor at the center of the tainted <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/immigration/2026/06/01/broadview-six-midway-blitz-abughazaleh-straw-rabbit-perry-trump-ice-crime" target="_blank" >“Broadview Six”</a> case as he moved to permanently drop charges<b> </b>in another case she handled where similar misconduct claims have surfaced.</p><p>Boutros personally filed a nine-page motion<b> </b>dropping<b> </b>charges<b> </b>tied to a 2018<b> </b>arson<b> </b>at a West Side grocery<b> </b>store, using the document to make the case that “the presumption of regularity to which [the government] is entitled under the law should not be shaken.”</p><p>The top prosecutor was referring to the legal principle that assumes federal officials are acting in good faith —<b> </b>a presumption that’s been <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2026/06/18/boutros-holleb-hotaling-atf-country-club-hills" target="_blank" >questioned by multiple judges</a> in recent weeks.</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2026/06/18/boutros-holleb-hotaling-atf-country-club-hills" >Charges dropped in suburban ATF sting, further straining trust between Boutros’ office and judges</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p>Ten defendants<b> </b>in three cases handled by Assistant U.S. Attorney Sheri Mecklenburg have now seen their federal charges permanently dropped as a result of the grand jury controversy in Boutros’ office. The defendants in the 2018 arson case were Alla<b> </b>Ishkirat, Tawfik<b> </b>“Mike”<b> </b>Salman, Larry<b> </b>Moneyham<b> </b>and<b> </b>Lonniel<b> </b>“Rudy” Nelson Jr.</p><p>U.S. District Judge Robert<b> </b>Gettleman<b> </b>granted<b> </b>Boutros’ motion<b> </b>shortly after it was filed.</p><p>The motion lays out several comments made by Mecklenburg to grand jurors<b> </b>that would appear inappropriate. They included Mecklenburg telling grand jurors she “can prove this case,”<b> </b>that<b> </b>“we don’t catch the smart ones,”<b> </b>that<b> </b>“most of them aren’t as smart as they think”<b> </b>and<b> </b>“the white-collar guys think they are the smartest in the world.”</p><p>The comments were apparently made without a court reporter present, because<b> </b>they’re<b> </b>“not contained in any transcript,”<b> </b>Boutros wrote. His office also reviewed “available audio,”<b> </b>his motion said.</p><p>Defense attorneys asked<b> </b>Gettleman<b> </b>to dismiss the charges last week, but Boutros made clear in his motion that “the U.S. attorney’s decision to dismiss with prejudice was also made before the defense filed their motion to dismiss on June 18, 2026.”</p><p>Boutros said his office will be conducting “an individualized review and assessment of all available grand jury minutes” of Mecklenburg’s Northern District of Illinois tenure<b> </b>since 2007, estimating that review will encompass “more than 100 grand jury cases.”</p><p>And, as part of an <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/immigration/2026/05/27/broadview-six-boutros-kat-abughazaleh-ice-trump-chicago-broadview" target="_blank" >ongoing reform process</a> in Boutros’ office, “under no circumstances are prosecutors to redact what they understand or perceive as the irrelevant portions of the transcripts submitted to the court for review,” he wrote.</p><p>“That way the court never receives redacted transcripts,” Boutros added.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure Defense attorneys have alleged a broader cover-up.</p><p>Christopher<b> </b>Parente, whose firm represents Ishkirat, raised doubts about Boutros’ latest announcement. Parente also represents Oak Park village trustee Brian<b> </b>Straw, who is among the former “Broadview Six” defendants.</p><p>“While I appreciate U.S. Attorney Boutros finally recognizing there is a credibility problem at his U.S. attorney’s office,” Parente said, “make no mistake that he and others had advance knowledge of these issues for months and did nothing to ‘remediate’ the problem when it became known to them and instead attempted to redact their way out of trouble.</p><p>“I do not trust those whose first instinct is to hide the truth to design the process of remediating its wrongs,” Parente added.</p><p>Parente and his co-counsel in the “Broadview Six” case have asked Perry to <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/immigration/2026/06/17/broadview-6-want-special-counsel-to-probe-boutros-office-trumps-justice-department-for-criminal-contempt" target="_blank" >appoint a special counsel</a> to investigate — and possibly prosecute — Boutros<b> </b>and other Justice Department officials in Chicago and Washington, D.C., for criminal contempt.</p><p>The four who saw their charges entries.title: Reviewing the Riverside-Brookfield summer shootout
entries.summary: <p>With the first high school basketball live period complete, here are a whole bunch of quick-hitting thoughts from the 84-team Riverside-Brookfield Shootout where over 125-plus college programs took in action.</p><p>■ There were two seniors that stood out from the rest as far as recruitable prospects, elevating their stock along the way: Benet’s Ed Stasys and Belleville West’s J’Dyn Lloyd. With so many departures to prep schools, the 6-8 Stasys and the 6-5 Lloyd are now two of the five best prospects in the Class of 2027.</p><p>Mid-major programs will keep their fingers crossed that Stasys stays at their level. He offers size, athleticism and the ability to really run and move while his defense and competitiveness puts him at an entirely distinct tier. That’s what will draw in college coaches from all levels.</p><p>Physically gifted and showing an improved face-up jumper, Lloyd visited Drake this past week and picked up an offer. The expectation is several more mid-major offers will be coming Lloyd’s way.</p><p>■ The two best prospects in the state, Bolingbrook’s Brady Pettigrew and Neuqua Valley’s Cole Kelly, are just juniors. But they remain the hottest commodities in the state and added more high-major offers following the weekend.</p><p>Pettigrew, who is now a consensus top 25 player in the Class of 2028, continues to polish his game and take it to an entirely different level.</p><p>■ There are few teams with as many pieces and quality depth as three teams in the expanded Catholic League: Benet, St. Laurence and St. Ignatius. All three went 4-0 on the weekend.</p><p>■ Speaking of St. Laurence, the red-hot spring of Markese Peoples extended into the June “live” period at Riverside-Brookfield. A physical terror offensively when he’s barreling downhill with the basketball, the 6-2 guard added offers from a pair of MAC schools, Toledo and Central Michigan.</p><p>■ Kendall Meyers is the lone returning starter for Class 4A state champ Marist. The versatile 6-5 wing is ready to shoulder a much bigger load as a senior. Meyers, along with a complement of young, up-and-coming players, led the RedHawks to a 4-0 record at R-B.</p><p>■ A new name to keep an eye on at Benet following a breakout weekend: Cormac Hanus. He’s a shooter with size on the perimeter. Hanus is a 6-5 senior and one of several unknown Benet players poised to contribute to what will again be one of the state’s top teams.</p><p>■ A freshman that really opened eyes and made a name for himself was Bloom’s Larry Ellis. The 6-2 guard dazzled at times and joins sophomores Kaden McClellan and Keiwon Gulley in a dynamite young backcourt.</p><p>■ East St. Louis, the defending Class 3A state champs, may have graduated one of the state’s top players in Saint Louis recruit Jamison White. But the Flyers, led by emerging seniors Phillip Jones and Terri’yon Webster, are loaded with talent and will be a state title contender again.</p><p>■ While it’s rare for Young not to have a big-named, highly-recruited player — Tennessee-bound Marquis Clark was the latest last season — the Dolphins look to be a team that will be better than people think. There is a nice blend of experience and youth. Coach Tyrone Slaughter’s team played hard and with a purpose in going 4-0 at R-B.</p><p>■ After a rock solid junior campaign this past season, Loyola’s Luke Alvarez is poised for a big senior year. In four games he averaged 22.8 points while shooting 46 percent from three with 21 made three-pointers. With high academics, the 6-1 guard should be a dream recruit for small college programs.</p><p>■ Oswego’s Ethan Vahl put up 31 points on Benet, something few players do. There are some efficiency questions to answer in some key areas, but there is no denying the talent he possesses in the backcourt.</p><p>■ He’s streaky, but when Crane’s Jamier Montgomery gets going on the offensive end, the 6-2 guard has shown to be a versatile and potent scorer. The creative and kinetic guard is lean and long, but he grabs your attention with his quick dribble-to-shoot motion.</p><p>■ Niles North guard Collin Tobin quietly put together a big junior year with little fanfare. A relative no-namer in the Class of 2027, the powerful guard opened eyes with his play at R-B and was one of the weekend’s big stock risers.</p><p>■ If this past weekend was any indication, Deerfield’s Tommy Donahue is set for a breakout season as a senior.</p><p>The 6-5 Donahue was a key player for a Deerfield team that reached the Class 3A state championship game last season, where it fell to East St. Louis. But he was a complementary player to Jake Pollack and Evan Nagler while averaging 6.7 points a game.</p><p>As clearly the go-to player for the Warriors this season, Donahue shined at R-B, making contested shots and drilling nine three-pointers in one game. He finished up the four games averaging more than 20 points a game.</p>

entries.title: Local leaders, advocates call for creation of Department of Gun Violence Reduction
entries.summary: <p>A coalition of city and county officials, as well as local advocates, are pushing for the creation of a new citywide Department of Gun Violence Reduction.</p><p>“This would create a stabilized department in the long term that isn’t just responding to the whims of today when we’re dealing with sustained issues,” said Deputy Mayor for Community Safety Emmanuel Andre on Monday during a press conference at City Hall.</p><p>Details were still scant on staffing or what the department would look like, but officials said it would have a $100 million budget made up of existing public safety money across city departments. It would also have contracting and procurement powers to put workers like violence interrupters on the city’s payroll, the group said.</p><p>The city plans to spend more than <a class="Link" href="https://www.chicago.gov/content/dam/city/depts/obm/supp_info/2026Budget/2026%20Budget%20Overview.pdf" target="_blank" >$3 billion on public safety this year</a>, meaning the proposal would take up about 3% of that spending.</p><p>The new proposal would replace the mayor’s Office of Community Safety, one of many existing city agencies and offices devoted to the issue. That office currently coordinates the city’s response to violence between the city’s first responders, emergency management, as well as the police board and oversight agencies.</p><p>In a statement, Mayor Brandon Johnson said he supported the creation of the office, which would "ensure [gun violence prevention] efforts are aligned, accountable and sustained over time."</p><p>Beth Brown, a pastor at Lincoln Park Presbyterian Church and former Interim Commissioner on the Community Commission for Public Safety and Accountability, said it would differ from other public safety agencies by more broadly coordinating the city’s strategy to combat violence, bringing housing, jobs programs and youth services into the fold.</p><p>“Gun violence prevention cannot be the effort of one department alone,” Brown said.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-e60000" name="image-e60000"></a>
